explanation: Forwards commit parties to a future transaction on agreed terms. Futures standardise contracts and usually use exchange clearing and daily settlement. Both create exposure without requiring payment of the underlying's full value at inception.
Daily settlement changes cash timing and can cause liquidity pressure before the final economic hedge benefit arrives. Contract size, expiry, delivery and basis need to match the user's exposure.

types.name: Forward
types.explanation: Bilateral customised commitment.

types.name: Future
types.explanation: Standardised contract with exchange mechanisms.

types.name: Long versus short
types.explanation: Obligation to buy or sell under terms.

workedCase.setup: A long forward buys an asset at ₹100 in one year. Ignore costs and discounting of settlement.
steps: At terminal price ₹120, payoff is ₹20.
At ₹80, payoff is −₹20.
A futures position can realise gains or losses through daily cash settlement before that date.
workedCase.result: A commitment has two-sided payoff exposure.
workedCase.interpretation: Collateral and counterparty terms change funding and failure risks.

explanation: A call gives its holder the specified right to buy; a put gives the right to sell. The buyer pays a premium for optionality, while the seller takes an obligation under the contract. Exercise style and settlement determine when and how rights can be used.
A purchased option's expiration payoff cannot be negative, but its profit can be negative because of premium and costs. A written option has a different risk profile.

types.name: Call
types.explanation: Right to buy at the strike.

types.name: Put
types.explanation: Right to sell at the strike.

types.name: Exercise style
types.explanation: European date-only or American eligible early exercise.

workedCase.setup: Buy a call with strike ₹100 and premium ₹7. Assume one unit and expiration price ₹120.
steps: Profit before financing and fees = ₹20 − ₹7 = ₹13.
At expiration price ₹95, payoff is zero and loss is ₹7.
workedCase.result: Optionality limits this buyer's expiration loss to the paid premium before other obligations.
workedCase.interpretation: Selling the option reverses its payoff and can create much larger exposure.

analysis: Read strike, size and exercise style.

explanation: A payoff diagram shows the contract's settlement value across underlying outcomes. A profit diagram also includes entry cost, premium and other specified expenses. Long and short positions have opposite contractual payoffs, but costs and financing can differ.
Combining instruments adds their payoffs at compatible dates and units. A diagram is not a probability distribution and says nothing by itself about which outcomes are likely.

types.name: Payoff
types.explanation: Terminal contract result.

types.name: Profit
types.explanation: Payoff less relevant entry and holding costs.

types.name: Break-even
types.explanation: Outcome where defined profit is zero.

workedCase.setup: A long call strikes at ₹100 and costs ₹7, ignoring interest and fees.
steps: At price ₹110, payoff is ₹10 and profit ₹3.
Break-even is ₹107.
At ₹100 or below, payoff is zero and profit −₹7.
workedCase.result: The strike and profit break-even are different prices.
workedCase.interpretation: Earlier market value depends on remaining time and volatility, not just the expiration diagram.

analysis: Do not interpret payoff shape as outcome probability.

explanation: Moneyness compares underlying or forward price with strike under a stated convention. Intrinsic value is the eligible immediate exercise value; time value is the remaining option value above that amount under the selected definition. Options can trade above intrinsic value before expiry.

In-the-money does not necessarily mean profitable after premium. European options cannot always be exercised immediately, and interest, dividends and settlement conventions affect nuanced comparisons.

types.name: In the money
types.explanation: Positive exercise-value relationship.

types.name: At the money
types.explanation: Near the selected price-strike reference.

types.name: Out of the money
types.explanation: No positive immediate intrinsic value.

workedCase.setup: A call's underlying is ₹108, strike ₹100 and market premium ₹12.
steps: Intrinsic value under the simple spot definition is ₹8.
Extrinsic value is ₹12 − ₹8 = ₹4.
A buyer paying ₹12 needs a sufficiently favourable outcome to recover premium and costs.
workedCase.result: Positive intrinsic value is not the same as positive trade profit.
workedCase.interpretation: The residual reflects time and other pricing factors.

analysis: Account for exercise and distribution terms.

explanation: Put-call parity links European calls and puts with the same underlying, strike and expiry to matched stock and cash positions. For a non-dividend-paying stock under standard assumptions, C + PV(K) = P + S. It follows from equal terminal payoffs.
Dividend, exercise, funding and settlement differences require adjustments. A price discrepancy after costs is not automatically a feasible arbitrage if shorting or financing is unavailable.

types.name: Protective put
types.explanation: Stock plus put.

types.name: Fiduciary call
types.explanation: Call plus cash to pay strike.

types.name: Adjusted parity
types.explanation: Incorporate relevant distributions and conventions.

workedCase.setup: Assume S ₹100, PV(K) ₹95 and call ₹12 for matching European options on a non-dividend stock.
steps: Parity requires P = 12 + 95 − 100 = ₹7.
Call plus strike cash costs ₹107.
Stock plus put also costs ₹107 and has the same terminal floor under the assumptions.
workedCase.result: The matched packages explain the price relation.
workedCase.interpretation: Real implementation requires equal rights, dates and feasible funding.

explanation: A binomial model represents possible up and down prices, then values a derivative by replication or risk-neutral probabilities under no-arbitrage assumptions. Risk-neutral probabilities are pricing weights, not claims about the actual likelihood of market moves.
Multiple periods approximate a richer path but still depend on volatility, timing and exercise rules. A valid model should reconcile the option with a self-financing replicating position.

types.name: Price tree
types.explanation: Possible underlying states.

types.name: Replication
types.explanation: Stock and cash reproduce derivative payoff.

types.name: Risk-neutral valuation
types.explanation: Discount payoff with model pricing weights.

workedCase.setup: Stock is ₹100 now and will be ₹120 or ₹80 in one period. Call strike ₹100; assume zero interest and no dividends.
steps: Call payoffs are ₹20 and zero.
Risk-neutral up weight is (100 − 80)/(120 − 80) = 0.5.
Option value = 0.5 × ₹20 = ₹10; half a share financed by ₹40 borrowing replicates it.
workedCase.result: The price does not require assuming actual up probability is 50%.
workedCase.interpretation: Costs, jumps and market constraints can invalidate simple replication.

explanation: Black-Scholes values a European option under assumptions including a specified continuous price process, constant parameters and frictionless replication. For a non-dividend stock, call value is S N(d1) − K e^−rT N(d2), with d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)T]/(σ√T) and d2 = d1 − σ√T.
The formula is a model, not proof that prices have constant volatility or no jumps. Dividends, early exercise, smiles and discrete hedging require extensions or different methods.

types.name: European model
types.explanation: Exercise at expiry.

types.name: Volatility input
types.explanation: Annualised parameter under the model.

types.name: Normal probability functions
types.explanation: N(d1) and N(d2) weight the replicated components.

workedCase.setup: Assume S = K = ₹100, r = 0, T = 1 year, σ = 20%, and no dividends.
steps: Using N(0.1) ≈ 0.53983 and N(−0.1) ≈ 0.46017, call value is about ₹7.97.
Stress volatility and compare market price rather than treating the output as certainty.
workedCase.result: Even at-the-money options have value before expiry.
workedCase.interpretation: Real risk includes model mismatch and hedging frictions.

explanation: Option Greeks describe local sensitivity to underlying price, time, volatility and rates. Delta is first-order price sensitivity; gamma is the change in delta; theta concerns time passage; vega concerns volatility; rho concerns rates. Sign and units depend on instrument and convention.
Greeks change as prices and time change. A delta hedge reduces one local exposure but leaves gamma, volatility, funding and gap risk.

types.name: Delta and gamma
types.explanation: First- and second-order underlying sensitivity.

types.name: Theta
types.explanation: Time sensitivity under a stated convention.

types.name: Vega
types.explanation: Volatility sensitivity.

types.name: Rho
types.explanation: Interest-rate sensitivity.

workedCase.setup: Assume delta 0.6 and gamma 0.04 per price unit. Underlying rises ₹2; ignore all other effects.
steps: Delta contribution ≈ 0.6 × 2 = ₹1.20.
Gamma contribution ≈ 0.5 × 0.04 × 2² = ₹0.08.
Second-order estimated option change is ₹1.28.
workedCase.result: The linear delta estimate misses curvature.
workedCase.interpretation: Large jumps and changing Greeks require direct repricing.

analysis: Stress nonlocal moves and other exposures.

explanation: Implied volatility is the parameter making a specified pricing model match an observed option price. Realised volatility measures historical price variability over a stated window and method. Their difference may reflect expectations, premiums, jumps and model limitations.
A high implied-realised gap does not guarantee a profitable short-volatility trade. Future realised volatility is unknown, and discrete hedging, direction and costs affect outcomes.

types.name: Historical realised volatility
types.explanation: Past measured variability.

types.name: Forecast volatility
types.explanation: Estimate of future variability.

types.name: Implied volatility
types.explanation: Price-inferred model input.

workedCase.setup: An option price implies 30% volatility; the previous month's realised measure is 20%.
steps: Verify horizon and annualisation are comparable.
Assess upcoming events and how the pricing model treats jumps.
Evaluate prospective rather than only past realised volatility.
workedCase.result: Two different measures need not converge simply because they are compared.
workedCase.interpretation: Trade outcome also depends on position Greeks, timing and implementation.

analysis: Separate past data from future uncertainty.

explanation: A volatility smile or skew shows different implied volatilities across strikes for the same expiry; a term structure shows differences across maturities. These patterns challenge a single constant-volatility representation and affect relative pricing and hedge behaviour.
Implied volatilities should be compared at consistent moneyness and timestamps. Bid-ask noise, illiquidity and differing exercise features can create misleading surfaces.

types.name: Smile
types.explanation: Both wings differ from the centre.

types.name: Skew
types.explanation: Asymmetric strike pattern.

types.name: Term structure
types.explanation: Volatility changes with expiry.

workedCase.setup: At one expiry, downside put implied volatility is 35%, at-the-money is 25% and upside call is 28%.
steps: The downside wing is especially elevated.
Assess tail protection demand and model conventions without claiming one unique cause.
Use a strike-aware surface instead of one 25% input for all contracts.
workedCase.result: Different strikes embed different prices for nonlinear exposure.
workedCase.interpretation: The surface must remain consistent with feasible option-price relationships.

analysis: Check surface consistency and event effects.

explanation: Option strategies combine positions to reshape payoff, premium and risk. Spreads limit selected exposures; straddles and strangles combine calls and puts for movement exposure; collars combine an underlying holding with protective and sold options. Labels do not determine whether a strategy suits a particular objective.
Calculate the entire package, including exercise and assignment obligations, rather than viewing one leg's gain in isolation.

types.name: Vertical spread
types.explanation: Same option type with different strikes.

types.name: Straddle or strangle
types.explanation: Call and put combine movement exposure.

types.name: Collar
types.explanation: Underlying plus downside protection and capped upside.

workedCase.setup: Buy a ₹100 strike call for ₹8 and sell a ₹110 call for ₹3, same expiry. Ignore fees.
steps: Net premium is ₹5.
At expiry price ₹120, spread payoff is ₹20 − ₹10 = ₹10 and profit ₹5.
At ₹95, payoff is zero and loss ₹5.
workedCase.result: The spread limits both this package's upside and downside under the assumptions.
workedCase.interpretation: Early exercise and different settlement can create additional mechanics.

analysis: Read exercise, assignment and collateral terms.

explanation: Swaps exchange specified payment streams, such as fixed for floating interest, one currency for another or fixed for variable commodity prices. Notional determines calculation size but is not always exchanged. Payment netting and principal exchange depend on terms.
A swap changes exposure rather than erasing risk. Basis, counterparty, collateral and termination costs can remain; a cross-currency swap also has currency funding mechanics.

types.name: Interest-rate swap
types.explanation: Fixed and floating interest streams.

types.name: Currency swap
types.explanation: Specified currency cash streams, potentially including principal.

types.name: Commodity swap
types.explanation: Fixed versus variable commodity pricing.

workedCase.setup: Assume ₹100 lakh notional, annual fixed payment 6% and floating receipt 8%, with net settlement and no principal exchange.
steps: Fixed leg is ₹6.
Floating leg is ₹8.
Net receipt is ₹2.
workedCase.result: The ₹100 notional is a calculation base rather than that year's receipt.
workedCase.interpretation: Different reset dates, day counts and collateral terms alter actual amounts.

analysis: Assess basis, credit and liquidity exposures.

explanation: A credit default swap exchanges premiums for specified protection following contractual credit events. Protection payment depends on notional, settlement and recovery conventions. Buying protection can offset a matching credit exposure or create a separate credit position.
The reference borrower and protection seller are different risk sources. A hedge can fail through mismatched events, maturity, seniority or counterparty default.

types.name: Protection buyer
types.explanation: Pays premium for specified credit-event benefit.

types.name: Protection seller
types.explanation: Receives premium and bears event obligation.

types.name: Reference exposure
types.explanation: Entity or obligation covered under terms.

workedCase.setup: Assume ₹100 lakh protection, a qualifying default and 40% recovery under simplified cash settlement.
steps: Protection payment is ₹100 × (1 − 40%) = ₹60.
Premiums paid are separate costs.
Check whether the buyer's bond loss and contract payout actually match.
workedCase.result: Protection is governed by events and settlement terms, not every price decline.
workedCase.interpretation: Accrued premiums, auction mechanics and counterparty risk can change results.

analysis: Assess premium, basis and seller risk.

explanation: Caps limit specified floating-rate payment exposure; floors provide a minimum rate-linked benefit; swaptions give the right to enter a specified swap. They are options, so premiums and exercise matter. A cap is often a sequence of period options rather than a single loan-rate reset.
Protection depends on benchmark, dates and notional matching. A borrower may still face loan-margin changes, fees or credit costs outside the cap.

types.name: Cap
types.explanation: Benefit when the eligible rate exceeds a strike.

types.name: Floor
types.explanation: Benefit when it falls below a strike.

types.name: Swaption
types.explanation: Option to enter a specified swap.

workedCase.setup: Assume a one-year cap period on ₹100 lakh at 4%, with realised eligible rate 6% and unit accrual factor.
steps: Rate difference is 2 percentage points.
Illustrative cap payment is ₹2 lakh before settlement timing effects.
Subtract the cap premium when assessing total economics.
workedCase.result: The option offsets benchmark-rate excess under the matched assumptions.
workedCase.interpretation: Actual contracts specify period accrual and payment dates.

explanation: Exotic options have features beyond a basic terminal call or put, such as barriers, averages, baskets or path-dependent conditions. Terminal underlying price alone may not determine payoff. Pricing requires a model reflecting the contractual path and dependence.
Complexity can hide exposure to gaps, observation frequency and correlations. A cheaper premium may reflect weaker protection, not a better version of the same contract.

types.name: Barrier option
types.explanation: Activation or cancellation at a defined threshold.

types.name: Asian option
types.explanation: Depends on an average.

types.name: Basket or path-dependent option
types.explanation: Multiple assets or historical path matter.

workedCase.setup: A knock-out call strikes at ₹100 and cancels if price touches ₹130. Assume continuous monitoring. It touches ₹130 then ends at ₹120.
steps: The barrier condition cancels the option.
Its payoff is zero under the stated terms.
A plain ₹100 call at the same terminal price would pay ₹20.
workedCase.result: Identical terminal prices can give different exotic payoffs.
workedCase.interpretation: Observation and rebate terms can change the example.

explanation: Structured notes combine an issuer debt claim with embedded derivative features. Return may depend on equity, rates, credit or barriers. Principal protection is a contractual promise under specified conditions, not necessarily protection against issuer default or an early sale loss.
Decompose the debt, option, fees and distribution terms. Headline coupons can compensate for sold optionality or tail exposure that is less visible than ordinary bond risk.

types.name: Debt component
types.explanation: Issuer repayment obligation.

types.name: Embedded derivative
types.explanation: Contingent market-linked payoff.

types.name: Conditional protection
types.explanation: Limits defined by maturity, barriers or issuer solvency.

workedCase.setup: Assume a ₹100 note promises principal at maturity plus an option-linked bonus, subject to issuer payment.
steps: If the market feature pays ₹20 and issuer performs, receipt is ₹120.
If the issuer defaults, the promised ₹100 may not be recovered fully.
Selling before maturity can produce a price below ₹100.
workedCase.result: Protection wording must be read with its conditions.
workedCase.interpretation: This is an illustrative structure, not a specific product recommendation.

analysis: Identify embedded option exposure and fees.

explanation: Hedging reduces an identified exposure; speculation intentionally accepts exposure for potential return; arbitrage seeks profit from inconsistently priced equivalent claims under stated constraints. The same derivative can serve any of these purposes depending on other positions and contracts.
Judge the combined position, not the instrument name. A hedge can have an isolated loss while successfully stabilising the underlying business cash flow.

types.name: Hedge
types.explanation: Offset an existing risk.

types.name: Speculation
types.explanation: Create or increase risk deliberately.

types.name: Arbitrage
types.explanation: Matched-payoff price inconsistency.

workedCase.setup: An exporter will receive $10,000 and sells matching dollars forward at ₹82. Assume quantity and date match.
steps: At ₹85 spot, the receipt alone is ₹850,000 but the forward offset reduces it to ₹820,000.
At ₹80, the combined amount is also ₹820,000 under the simplified settlement.
Evaluate the stable combined receipt rather than the derivative alone.
workedCase.result: A hedge trades favourable upside for greater predictability.
workedCase.interpretation: Forecast cancellation or timing changes create residual exposure.

explanation: Margin and collateral support performance of derivatives and leveraged positions. Initial margin covers specified potential exposure; variation margin responds to value changes. Clearing changes the counterparty structure but does not eliminate liquidity, default or operational risk.
Margin is not the maximum economic loss. A position can require additional cash rapidly, and a sound long-term hedge can fail if the user cannot fund interim calls.

types.name: Initial margin
types.explanation: Starting or modelled exposure support.

types.name: Variation margin
types.explanation: Settlement or collateral for value changes.

types.name: Clearing and bilateral risk
types.explanation: Different default-management structures.

workedCase.setup: A futures position has ₹100 lakh economic exposure and initial margin ₹10. An adverse move creates a ₹6 cash settlement.
steps: The user must fund the ₹6 under contract rules.
The original ₹10 is not a guarantee that losses stop there.
Stress further moves and available liquidity.
workedCase.result: Low initial cash commitment can hide large cash-call risk.
workedCase.interpretation: Collateral eligibility and haircuts affect actual funding needs.

analysis: Read clearing, default and collateral rules.

explanation: Basis risk arises when a hedge and underlying exposure do not move identically. Differences can involve product, location, credit, maturity or benchmark. Hedge effectiveness assesses the offset under a defined economic or accounting purpose.
Historical correlation does not guarantee future offset. Quantity changes, nonlinear exposures and sudden market dislocations can create larger residual losses than ordinary-period estimates suggest.

types.name: Price basis
types.explanation: Different related instruments.

types.name: Timing basis
types.explanation: Mismatched dates or reset periods.

types.name: Quantity or credit basis
types.explanation: Exposure amount or payment source differs.

workedCase.setup: A fuel buyer's actual cost rises ₹10 lakh, while a related commodity hedge gains ₹8.
steps: Unhedged shock is ₹10.
Hedge offsets ₹8.
Residual loss is ₹2 before premiums, funding and other costs.
workedCase.result: An imperfect hedge reduces risk without removing it.
workedCase.interpretation: A different shock can change the relationship; effectiveness needs scenario testing.

analysis: Assess total economics and accounting qualification separately.

explanation: A derivative's value depends on an underlying price, rate, index or other specified variable. Read the contract's obligations, exercise rights, cash settlement, maturity and collateral requirements before calculating a payoff. Payoff at maturity differs from profit after premiums, financing and transaction costs.

A hedge reduces a defined exposure; it may leave basis risk, volume uncertainty or counterparty risk. Leverage can arise because a small premium or margin controls a larger economic exposure. Pricing assumptions, volatility, Greeks and liquidity matter before maturity even when the terminal payoff formula is simple.

types.name: Forward or future
types.explanation: A contractual exposure to a future exchange or settlement, with differing clearing and margin structures.

types.name: Option
types.explanation: A right whose holder and writer have different asymmetric obligations.

types.name: Swap
types.explanation: An exchange of specified payment streams.

types.name: Structured product
types.explanation: A combined claim whose embedded features must be decomposed.

workedCase.setup: Buy a call with strike ₹100 for ₹8 premium. At expiry, consider underlying prices ₹90, ₹105 and ₹120; ignore financing and costs.
steps: Call payoff = max(price − ₹100, 0).
Payoffs are ₹0, ₹5 and ₹20.
Profits after premium are −₹8, −₹3 and ₹12.
workedCase.result: An in-the-money option at ₹105 still loses ₹3 after the initial premium.
workedCase.interpretation: The break-even terminal price is ₹108 under these assumptions. Interim option value and writer risk require additional analysis.

analysis: Calculate payoff, premium and cash funding separately.
Test hedge basis, collateral and counterparty risks.
